observations.name: diagnosis
observations.output:
Revenue rose 6.03% over the 68-hour window from 2026-06-28 04:00 to 2026-06-30 23:00. The movement is essentially entirely a request-volume story: requests came in at 780,742 against a baseline of 733,766, up 6.4%, accounting for 105.99% of the total movement. The other factors barely moved — fill rate 0.7758 vs 0.7846 (-1.12%, -19.24% of movement), eCPM 2.4914 vs 2.4716 (+0.8%, +13.63%), and render rate 0.9798 vs 0.98 (-0.02%).

No segment is responsible — the change was global. Every dimension tested came back uniform: vertical (all 8 values within 4.3% of the global +6.4%), device_model (8 values within 0.8%), os_version (8 within 0.9%), country (16 within 1.8%), ad_format (5 within 0.6%), region (5 within 0.3%), category (7 within 0.7%), and publisher_tier (3 within 0.1%). The shape was gradual, not a step: onset at 2026-06-28 05:00 took hourly requests from 8,610 to 9,723 (+1,113), with the largest single hour carrying only 24.4% of the change; recovery was likewise gradual from 2026-07-01 04:00 (9,598 to 10,719, +1,121, step fraction 61.16%), and neither boundary aligned to a day boundary. Interpretation: this ramp profile is consistent with a rollout or progressive change in upstream request volume rather than a single discrete switch.

Ruled out: campaign_type was inconclusive — CPM leads the dimension but its excess is 0% of the unexplained movement, below the 50% concentration bar, and it explains only 9% of the incident, under the 10% materiality bar. All other dimensions were uniform, with largest outliers explaining between 0.2% and 4.5% of the incident. Because fill_rate, render_rate and eCPM held steady throughout, a supply or demand-quality problem is excluded — everything that arrived filled and rendered normally, so the change is purely in how many requests arrived. Next step is to look upstream of the auction at traffic sources and SDK/app-side request generation, and at anything rolling out progressively starting around 2026-06-28 05:00 and unwinding around 2026-07-01 04:00.

observations.name: diagnosis
observations.output:
Revenue fell 44.81% over the 24-hour window from 2026-06-21 00:00:00 to 2026-06-21 23:00:00. The movement is almost entirely an upstream volume story: requests came in at 126,052 against a baseline of 223,079, a 43.49% decline accounting for 96.03% of the total movement. eCPM contributed marginally at 2.4186 vs 2.4771 baseline (-2.36%, 4.02% of movement), while fill rate (0.7855 vs 0.7849, +0.08%) and render rate (0.9794 vs 0.9798, -0.05%) were flat.

No segment is responsible — the drop was uniform across every dimension tested. The shape is a clean switch, not a degradation: requests stepped from 6,503 to 3,651 within the single hour at 2026-06-21 00:00:00, with 100% of the movement landing in that one hour, exactly on a day boundary. It reversed just as sharply at 2026-06-22 00:00:00, from 3,603 to 8,132, after exactly one day. Fill rate, render rate and eCPM held steady throughout. Interpretation: this pattern is consistent with something that schedules in whole days — a campaign flight with a defined end date, a config push, or a nightly job — rather than an organic failure or a fix.

Ruled out: publisher_tier (3 values, all within 0.7% of global -43.5%), ad_format (5 values, within 1.0%), category (7 values, within 1.4%), vertical (8 values, within 2.2%), os_version (8 values, within 0.8%), device_model (8 values, within 1.0%), region (5 values, within 0.7%), country (16 values, within 2.9%), and campaign_type (4 values, within 0.2%) — in every case the largest outlier explains 0.3% or less of the incident. The evidence also rules out a supply- or demand-quality problem: everything that did arrive filled and rendered normally, so the issue is that fewer requests arrived at all. Next step: check what was scheduled to start and end on 2026-06-21 — campaign flight dates, traffic-shaping or budget configs pushed at midnight, and any nightly job that ran once and reverted.

Between 2026-06-23 00:00:00 and 2026-06-25 23:00:00 (72 hours), revenue was essentially flat at -0.002%, but fill rate fell 4.4%, from a baseline of 0.7854 to 0.7508, accounting for 22.2% of the movement. The other factors did not contribute: requests were up 4.4% (843,741 vs 808,472 baseline, share -21.1%), eCPM was effectively unchanged at 2.4756 vs 2.4748 (+0.03%), and render rate was flat at 0.9801.

The movement is localized to fill rate on os_version = Android 15, which moved -44.9% against -4.4% globally, carrying 100% of the unexplained movement and 88% of the whole incident. A secondary concentration appears in region = EU, which moved -7.1% and accounts for 15% of the incident. The shape is a clean step, not a slide: fill rate for Android 15 went from 0.7846 to 0.4439 within the single hour at 2026-06-23 00:00:00, with 96% of the total movement landing in that hour, exactly on a day boundary. It reversed just as sharply at 2026-06-26 00:00:00 (0.4310 to 0.7962, step fraction 1.0) after exactly 3 days, while requests, render_rate and eCPM held steady throughout. Interpretation: a step on a day boundary that reverses after a whole number of days is consistent with something that schedules in days — a campaign flight with a defined end date, a config push, or a nightly job — rather than an organic degradation or a fix.

Checked and cleared: publisher_tier was uniform (all 3 values within 0.2% of the global -4.4%; largest outlier explains 1.6% of the incident), ad_format uniform (all 5 within 0.4%; largest outlier 1.5%), and category uniform (all 7 within 0.5%; largest outlier 1.4%). device_model and country were inconclusive — Redmi Note 12 leads device_model with 31% of unexplained movement and ES leads country with 29%, both under the 50% concentration bar, and ES explains only 7% of the incident, under the 10% materiality bar. vertical and campaign_type are not applicable, since every value holds the same fill rate. The evidence also rules out a traffic or tracking problem: request volume was unchanged, so the same demand arrived and was handled differently. Next, pull the Android 15 demand-side configuration and any campaign flights or targeting rules with a 2026-06-23 to 2026-06-26 date range, and check the EU concentration against the same schedule.
